briefs.label: Morning Brief
briefs.title: Tax Fallout, Ballot Politics, and a DEA Judge's Pen: Cannabis at a Crossroads
briefs.top: Michigan's 24% wholesale tax keeps bleeding storefronts and jobs even as it becomes a 2026 governor's-race wedge issue, while federally the DEA rescheduling fight has moved to closing arguments with a judge's recommendation looming. On the psychedelics side, Compass Pathways is deepening its federal footprint via a VA trial as Lykos regroups under a new name after last year's MDMA rejection.

local.text: GOP gubernatorial nominee John James unveiled a platform pledging to repeal or sharply cut the 24% wholesale cannabis tax while cracking down on unregulated delta-8/THCA products sold outside licensed dispensaries, arguing the tax "drives up prices, gives illegal operators a competitive edge, and has already fallen far short of revenue projections."

Upper Peninsula chain Higher Love shut five of its nine dispensaries (Crystal Falls, Escanaba, Houghton, Munising, Ontonagon) as of Aug. 9, with the company citing the mounting wholesale tax burden as the primary driver of the closures.

The 24% wholesale tax collected only about $34 million in its first months against a projected $420 million annual pace, and now faces two unresolved MiCIA lawsuits — one over the Legislature's supermajority requirement, another alleging unconstitutional "tax pyramiding" — keeping the industry's finances under active pressure heading into fall.

In back-to-back rulings, the Michigan Supreme Court held that a marijuana civil infraction alone can't justify a warrantless vehicle search (People v. Wilkins, 5-2) and that courts can't bar MRTMA-compliant use as a probation condition just because it violates federal law (People v. Hess, unanimous) — raising the evidentiary bar for cannabis-related traffic stops statewide.

Michigan remains the nation's cheapest legal market, with the lowest advertised ounce at $6.99 versus $112 in neighboring Ohio, a price gap analysts say keeps driving Ohio consumers across the border despite Ohio's new ban on out-of-state purchases.

national.text: DEA formally urged its own administrative law judge to recommend moving marijuana from Schedule I to Schedule III in an Aug. 17 post-hearing brief, while opposition groups including SAM and the states of Idaho, Indiana and Nebraska filed competing briefs asking the judge to reject rescheduling — setting up Judge Derek Julius's recommendation.
Judge Julius ordered a lengthy round of corrections to the official rescheduling-hearing transcript — reportedly at least 2,470 pages — with a finalized version due to be publicly posted by Aug. 26.

The Senate's Aug. 8 continuing resolution pushed the federal hemp-THC ban (originally effective Nov. 12) to Dec. 11, but the House hasn't acted yet, returns Aug. 31, and must fund the government by Sept. 30 — leaving the fate of the roughly $30 billion hemp industry unresolved.

Compass Pathways is partnering with the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs on PIVOT, a multi-site randomized controlled trial testing its COMP360 psilocybin in veterans with treatment-resistant depression, including those with co-occurring PTSD, deepening federal engagement with psychedelic-assisted therapy.

MDMA drug developer Lykos Therapeutics has quietly rebranded as Resilient Pharmaceuticals following a $50 million recapitalization and new executive team, an effort to shed the stigma of last year's FDA rejection of its PTSD therapy.
